name: Two-factor authentication (TOTP)
needs: require a code from an app after the password
lost my authenticator device and can't log in
summary: After the password, the user types a 6-digit code from an authenticator app. You store a secret per user, check codes with a small time window, and give recovery codes for when the phone is gone.
need_when: Accounts hold money, private data, or admin power.
Business customers ask for it in security reviews.
skip_when: You only use social login or passkeys, where the provider or device already covers this.

ways.title: Your auth library's MFA module
ways.how: django-allauth MFA, Devise two-factor, Better Auth's two-factor plugin, Laravel Fortify.
ways.tradeoff: Tested flows for setup, login and recovery. You follow its screens and storage.

ways.title: A hosted auth provider
ways.how: Clerk, Auth0, Supabase Auth, Firebase Auth and WorkOS offer TOTP and often SMS or passkeys.
ways.tradeoff: Minutes to turn on. Check which plan includes it.

ways.title: Build it with a TOTP library
ways.how: pyotp or otplib for codes, a QR code library for setup, your own tables for secrets and recovery codes.
ways.tradeoff: Full control. Easy to miss replay checks, rate limits and recovery.

prompt:
Add optional TOTP two-factor authentication, required for [admins].

Requirements:
- Setup: show a QR code and the secret as text, ask for one valid code before turning it on.
- Store the TOTP secret encrypted. Accept the current code and one step either side (30 seconds) and reject a code that was already used.
- Generate 10 single-use recovery codes, show them once, store only hashes.
- Login: after a correct password, ask for a code or a recovery code. Don't create the full session until it passes.
- Rate limit code attempts per account and per IP.
- Turning 2FA off or making new recovery codes needs the password plus a current code.
- Email the user whenever 2FA is turned on, off, or a recovery code is used.
- Password reset must not turn off 2FA.

Acceptance checks (run each and show me the result):
1. A code from Google Authenticator or 1Password logs in; the same code a second time fails.
2. Each recovery code works once.
3. Ten wrong codes in a row get throttled.
4. Resetting the password still asks for the second factor at login.
5. The database holds no plain recovery codes.
acceptance_checks: A code from Google Authenticator or 1Password logs in; the same code a second time fails.
Ten wrong codes in a row get throttled.
Resetting the password still asks for the second factor at login.
The database holds no plain recovery codes.
if_you_skip_it: One leaked password is enough to take over an account, or users lock themselves out with no way back.
